newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-JAPAN AND SOUTH KOREA REACH AGREEMENT ON "MAJOR ISSUES".
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-JAPAN AND SOUTH KOREA REACH AGREEMENT ON "MAJOR ISSUES".

text.p: Japan and South Korea said on Wednesday they had reached agreement on the "major issues" concerning the 2002 World Cup finals -- but FIFA and both co-hosts refused to say what those agreements were.

The only detail to emerge from a three-hour meeting of the 2002 Study Group was that the finals would comprise 32 teams and 64 matches and would not be increased to 40 teams, an idea Japan floated last month.
The meeting, chaired by Sweden's Lennart Johansson, agreed to recommend six key issues to FIFA's Executive Committee which meets in Barcelaona on December 7.

They were: the venue of the final, the name of the event, the event logo and mascot, the composition of the organising committee, the location of the main media and broadcasting centres and where the various draws would be held.
A plan to have a two-leg final was not backed and a South Korean plan to draw for where the final and opening matches would be held was not pursued by the committee.
Asked whether he was pleased about the decision on where to stage the final, Japan Football Association president Ken Naganuma said: "I am neither happy nor unhappy."
His South Korean counterpart, Chung Moon Jong, said: "It was a very productive meeting and we are all very happy at the outcome."

Alan Rothenberg, chief executive of the 1994 World Cup in the United States and a technical delegate to the Zurich meeting, said: "I am sworn to secrecy as is the rest of the committee. We have only made recommendations today for the Executive Committee to endorse next month."
